subject: British History
title: 1. The Glorious Revolution, William and Mary, and Queen Anne

segments.text: This is the foundation topic for Britain’s entire constitutional development: it establishes the pattern of limited, parliamentary monarchy that every later topic in this subject assumes as its starting point.

James II’s Catholic faith, his use of royal prerogative to relax legal restrictions on Catholics, and — decisively — the 1688 birth of a Catholic male heir who threatened a lasting Catholic dynasty, alarmed Protestant political leaders enough that a group of them invited James’s Protestant son-in-law, William of Orange (married to James’s daughter Mary), to intervene militarily. William landed with an army; James’s support collapsed and he fled to France. Parliament then offered the crown jointly to William and Mary on explicit constitutional conditions rather than as an unconditional restoration of royal authority. The

condemned specific abuses of royal power and strengthened Parliament’s role over taxation, legislation, and the maintenance of a standing army — a genuinely significant shift, though not the creation of full modern democracy: political participation remained narrow and property-based, and the monarchy retained real, if now more limited, influence for a long time afterward.

Prepare causes under religion, succession, royal power and parliamentary politics; then list constitutional results and explain why 1688–89 mattered for limited monarchy without claiming it created modern democracy.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did the 1688–89 settlement change the relationship between Crown and Parliament, and what remained unchanged?”
Do not call the Glorious Revolution a modern democratic revolution; the electorate remained narrow and property-based.
Do not confuse the Bill of Rights 1689 with the later American Bill of Rights.
Do not treat the 1707 union as the same event as the 1603 Union of the Crowns (Topic 3 clarifies this distinction fully).
James II’s Catholicism and use of royal prerogative generated strong opposition among political elites.
William of Orange landed in England in 1688; James II ultimately fled to France.
The Bill of Rights 1689 limited certain royal powers and strengthened Parliament’s constitutional position.
Queen Anne reigned from 1702 to 1714 and presided during the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Acts of Union 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain by uniting the English and Scottish parliaments.
1688–89 established limited, parliamentary monarchy through elite political conflict, not mass democratic revolution — a distinction every later topic in this subject depends on.

War financing under William III directly built lasting fiscal-administrative institutions (the Bank of England among them), establishing a war-drives-institutional-development pattern that recurs throughout British history.
Queen Anne’s reign carries the 1689 settlement into durable party politics and the 1707 union with Scotland, directly bridging into Topic 3.
